=== LDS_EcoPartner_Comments_PUC_58481.docx ===
BEFORE THE
PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS


COMMENTS OF LANDMARK DEVELOPMENT SERVICES
AND ECOPARTNER ALLIANCE

I.  Introduction
Landmark Development Services LLC (“Landmark”) and EcoPartner Alliance respectfully submit these comments in response to the Proposal for Publication of proposed 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load Interconnection Standards) in PUC Project No. 58481, and related proceedings PGRR145 and PUC Project No. 58484 (as noted). Landmark appreciates the Commission’s and Staff’s substantial effort to implement Senate Bill 6 and establish a structured, transparent framework for large load interconnection in ERCOT.

These comments address the proposed rule across five areas: (1) financial security and deposit rules; (2) SB 6 equipment pathways, behind-the-meter power, and curtailment; (3) process timelines and batch structure; (4) governance, appeals, and cost allocation; and (5) economic, community, and grid resilience considerations. Where a comment applies to multiple proceedings, it is tagged accordingly.

Docket Key
[58481]  PUC Project 58481 — Large Load Interconnection Standards (PUCT Substantive Rulemaking)
[PGRR145]  PGRR145 — ERCOT Planning Guide Revision / Batch Zero Process
[58484]  PUC Project 58484 — 4CP / Transmission Cost Allocation
[ALL]  Applies to all three proceedings / cross-cutting

II.  Financial Security & Deposit Rules
1. Financial Security — Deposit Structure Waterfall & Refundability  [58481] [58484]
The current framework stacks multiple financial obligations (IA security, IX fee, CIAC, and system upgrade security) without a published waterfall showing how they credit against each other. This creates significant uncertainty for developers and their financing partners. Landmark/EcoPartner recommends:
The financial security posted at the Intermediate Agreement stage should be fully refundable prior to any transmission planning studies being completed. At IA execution, there is zero line of sight to energization.
The draft PFP currently makes only 20% of the $100,000/MW IA security refundable. Retaining 80% of remaining funds after cost recovery operates as a penalty, not a cost recovery mechanism.
Clarity is needed on: (1) whether the IX fee was reduced from $100K/MW in the latest draft; and (2) a published waterfall table showing the order in which IA security, IX fee, CIAC, and system upgrade security apply and credit against each other. Developers cannot model total exposure without this.
Recommended refund structure: Outside of documented engineering costs, IA security should be 100% refundable until the 30-day steady-state screening window. After that, $6.5M becomes non-refundable as a continuation commitment, consistent with stated TSP materials and supplies cost estimates.
After applying outstanding costs, the balance should be fully refunded — not forfeited to the TSP as a rate base offset. The 80/20 retention-to-refund split in the draft is inconsistent with cost causation principles.
2. Deposit Uniformity Across TSP Pathways (NOIE vs. Direct Oncor)  [58481] [ALL]
Developers routing through a NOIE (e.g., Brazos Electric) face materially different financial security requirements and process clarity than those connecting directly through Oncor or AEP. This is not reflected in the current draft rule.
Financial security requirements and process clarity should be standardized whether a project connects through a NOIE pathway or a direct TSP pathway.
Currently, local utilities appear to require more upfront without clear published rules governing those requirements. This creates unequal treatment across a developer’s portfolio.
The Commission should require uniform deposit standards, refundability terms, and timeline obligations regardless of whether the interconnecting utility is a NOIE, co-op, or investor-owned utility.
3. Deposit Refund Mechanism — Escrow & Financing Community Clarity  [58481] [58484]
Rules on refundability if a project does not proceed are still being finalized and are not yet crystal clear. This is a material blocker for the financing community.
The Commission should establish firm escrow rules and a clear refund timeline before Batch Zero IA deadlines arrive (July 10, 2026).
Guidance should address: (1) escrow account structure, (2) which costs may be drawn from security vs. charged separately, and (3) timeline for refund processing after withdrawal or project cancellation.
Interest-bearing treatment for deposits held beyond a defined period should be required, consistent with PUC retail/residential deposit precedent.

III.  SB 6, Behind-the-Meter Power & Curtailment
4. 30-Minute Curtailment — Codify or Clarify Source  [58481] [PGRR145]
The 30-minute curtailment capability requirement needs to be clearly codified. PGRR145 Section 9.2.5 requires breakers under remote TO control but does not specify a time window. It is currently unclear whether “30 minutes” comes from the rule text or from informal TSP conversations.
If 30 minutes is not yet codified, Landmark/EcoPartner recommends it be formalized as a design standard in the final rule.
Implementation guidance is needed on what constitutes compliant equipment: switchgear standards, substation controls, dispatch programming, and curtailment response verification.
Projects should be able to demonstrate that BTM storage provides sufficient minimum load coverage during curtailment events to protect customer operations.
Clarity on this requirement is needed before developers can finalize equipment specifications. OEMs are currently willing to provide letters and allocations without deposits as a mechanism for demonstrating compliance — this should be formally recognized by the Commission.
5. SB 6 Equipment Proof Requirements — Formalize the Pathway  [58481]
The rules for how developers demonstrate 30-minute curtailment capability and BTM equipment pathways need to be clarified and formalized.
The Commission should define acceptable forms of equipment pathway demonstration: (1) executed purchase orders or deposits, (2) OEM allocation letters, and (3) signed LOIs with part numbers and delivery timelines.
OEM allocation letters without deposits are currently being offered as a market mechanism to support project inclusion in Batch Zero. This mechanism should be formally recognized as a valid pathway.
Equipment pathway requirements should not require full capital commitment at IA execution — the standard should reflect actual market conditions for long-lead equipment.
6. BTM Matching — Define Qualifying Resources  [58481]
If a percentage match between grid load and behind-the-meter generation is required under SB 6, the rule must explicitly define what resources qualify.
Battery storage (BESS) should explicitly count as a qualifying BTM resource for matching purposes. Projects combining natural gas, solar, and BESS should face no ambiguity.
The Commission should clarify whether the match requirement is applied at peak load, average load, or a defined minimum threshold.
7. BTM Power as Grid Resilience — Not a Grid Burden  [58481] [ALL]
Projects with on-site BTM generation actively contribute to ERCOT grid resilience by providing backup capacity and reducing net demand pressure during peak events.
These are not projects that simply consume from the grid — they add redundancy and, in curtailment scenarios, can shift load to BTM sources, relieving transmission stress.
The Commission should acknowledge in the rule’s findings that BTM generation associated with large load projects contributes positively to ERCOT reliability.

IV.  Process, Timelines & Batch Structure
8. Utility & ERCOT Response Timelines — Fill the Gaps  [58481] [PGRR145]
The draft imposes detailed milestone obligations on large load customers but is largely silent on reciprocal response timelines for utilities and ERCOT. Specific gaps include:
No timeline for ERCOT study validity determinations under PGRR145 Section 9.2.1.4.
No enforcement consequence if TSPs miss short-circuit study deadlines during the Batch Refinement phase.
No enforcement on the 15-business-day cost estimate requirement in Section 9.5.1(3).
Recommended minimum standards: (1) first substantive utility response within 60–90 days of application; (2) final formal decision within 6 months; (3) published milestone clock with automatic escalation to ERCOT if missed.
9. RTP vs. Batch Zero Relationship — Codify the Connection  [PGRR145] [58481]
The formal relationship between a TSP’s Regional Transmission Planning (RTP) process and Batch Zero eligibility is currently unclear. ERCOT staff have indicated these processes are “separate,” but that has not been codified publicly.
The Commission and ERCOT should publish a clear statement on whether RTP participation or non-participation affects a project’s Batch Zero standing, queue position, or study validity.
Overlapping dependencies between the rulemaking and the ERCOT planning guide create developer uncertainty. The Commission should create a coordination plan to harmonize Project 58481 substantive rules with PGRR145 reforms prior to the ERCOT Board vote.
10. MW Allocation Criteria for Studied Load — Section 9.3.2  [PGRR145]
Section 9.3.2 gives ERCOT discretion to allocate MW among competing loads in the same corridor but provides no published criteria for prioritization.
The ordering provisions in Section 9.2.1.4 cover base load scenarios only. Competing loads in constrained corridors have no published priority framework.
ERCOT should publish criteria for MW allocation decisions, including tie-breaking rules, transparency reporting, and whether BTM generation capability is a factor.
11. Batch One Committed Timeline — Close the Limbo Gap  [PGRR145]
Loads that miss Batch Zero are effectively in limbo indefinitely under the current framework. Section 9.2.1(4) references “future PGRR” for Batch One, but this is non-binding.
ERCOT should commit to a published Batch One opening date as part of the Batch Zero final report, no later than Q3 2027.
The absence of a Batch One timeline discourages developers from completing projects that miss Batch Zero by narrow margins, reducing overall investment.
12. Substantially Similar Interconnection Disclosure — Clarify Scope  [58481]
Section 9.7.1(b) requires disclosure of substantially similar parallel IX requests, with “material change” defined as a 20% demand change or 1-year delay. Two gaps need addressing:
Per-entity vs. per-site applicability: Does the disclosure obligation apply at the entity level or per site? Affiliated entities with multiple sites need clear guidance.
Electrically unrelated corridors: Should a project in a different load zone or transmission corridor trigger the substantially similar disclosure? The current language is ambiguous.

V.  Governance, Appeals & Cost Allocation
13. Appeal Mechanism for Study Validity Determinations  [PGRR145] [58481]
Section 9.2.1.4(2) gives ERCOT sole authority over study validity determinations with no appeal path, no published timeline, and no published criteria.
A defined review timeline and dispute resolution process should be established for study validity determinations.
Developers should have a right to request an independent review of ERCOT’s validity determination within a defined window (suggest 30 days), with a response required within 60 days.
14. CLR / Provisional CLR Mechanics — Financial Security & Queue Priority  [PGRR145] [58481]
Workshop 6 introduced Provisional CLR (partial firm plus curtailable). Several open questions need resolution before CLR/PCLR designations are relied upon for project structuring:
Does financial security scale to the firm portion only, or to full contracted peak demand?
How does PCLR designation interact with the Qualifying Schedule Agreement (QSA)?
Do curtailable MW under a PCLR receive priority in future batches, or do they reset to the back of the queue?
CLR designation should be treated as a pathway to expedite energization for already-approved loads — not as a mechanism to gain grid capacity allocation before controllability has been validated by the ERCOT process.
15. Cross-TO Cost Allocation Methodology — Section 9.7.2(j)  [PGRR145] [58484]
Section 9.7.2(j) requires financial security for system upgrades but does not define how costs are allocated when upgrades span multiple transmission owners or provide system-wide benefits.
A published cost allocation methodology should be required before financial security for cross-TO upgrades can be reasonably posted.
Costs that provide broad system benefits should not be assigned entirely to the triggering large load customer. The methodology should reflect cost causation principles.
This point overlaps directly with Project 58484 (4CP/transmission cost allocation) — coordination between comment positions in both dockets is recommended.
16. Grandfathering — Projects with Executed Agreements Pre-Effective Date  [58481]
Any project that has executed a signed agreement with the TSP prior to the effective date of the final rule and has satisfied all CIAC and financial security obligations per the terms of that agreement should be exempt from additional costs or security requirements imposed by the new standards.
Projects that have already committed capital and executed agreements should not be retroactively subject to new deposit or compliance requirements.
17. Site Control — Option to Purchase Should Qualify  [58481]
The option to purchase should be retained as a valid form of site control for the Intermediate Agreement criteria.
A legally binding option to purchase or lease for the proposed load location should satisfy the site control requirement at the IA stage.
Deal structures that include the right to purchase through direct contracts with landowners should qualify without requiring a fully executed deed or lease at IA execution.

VI.  Economic, Community & Grid Resilience Considerations
18. Workforce & Economic Development — Power Plant + Data Center Jobs  [ALL]
These are not standard data center builds. Co-locating a power plant with a data center creates a materially larger workforce and economic footprint than a typical colocation or hyperscale facility.
Workforce includes: grid operators, gas plant operations staff, cooling infrastructure technicians, construction trades, and permanent data center staff.
This is a significant economic development argument, particularly for rural Texas counties. Local community support in multiple counties reflects this dynamic.
These projects should be framed explicitly as power plant and data center joint developments, not data centers that happen to have backup power.
19. On-Site Water Resources — Community Impact  [ALL]
Landmark/EcoPartner projects are designed to leverage on-site water resources and avoid impact to community water supply.
This should be noted as a project design standard and differentiator from large-scale data center projects that rely entirely on municipal water.
Water use is a growing public concern in Texas data center discussions — proactively addressing it in the regulatory record protects project sentiment and provides the Commission with evidence of responsible development practices.

VII.  Conclusion
Landmark Development Services and EcoPartner Alliance appreciate the opportunity to submit these comments. The Commission’s implementation of SB 6 through proposed 16 TAC §25.194 is a critical step toward establishing a transparent, predictable, and durable framework for large load interconnection in ERCOT. Landmark and EcoPartner urge the Commission to address the specific concerns and recommendations outlined above to ensure the final rule supports responsible development while maintaining system reliability.

Respectfully submitted,
